name: MathlibAnnex.Sphere.radialExtension_integral_abs_det
title: The absolute Jacobian integral of a radial sphere extension

content.display_title: The absolute Jacobian integral of a radial sphere extension
content.one_sentence_role: Identifies the integral of the absolute Jacobian over an open source unit ball with the volume of the closed target unit ball.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $m\in\mathbb N_0$, put $n=m+1$, and let $E=\mathbb R^n$ have its standard sup norm $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and Lebesgue measure $\lambda$. Let $p,q$ be continuous seminorms on $E$ with specified positive constants $a_p,b_p,a_q,b_q$ satisfying
$$a_p\|x\|_\infty\le p(x)\le b_p\|x\|_\infty,\qquad a_q\|x\|_\infty\le q(x)\le b_q\|x\|_\infty\quad(x\in E).$$
The lower bounds make $p$ and $q$ norms. Define their unit spheres by $\Sigma_p=\{x:p(x)=1\}$ and $\Sigma_q=\{y:q(y)=1\}$. Let $\Delta:\Sigma_p\to\Sigma_q$ be a bijection satisfying
$$q(\Delta(u)-\Delta(v))=p(u-v)\qquad(u,v\in\Sigma_p).$$
Its radial extension, read as a map $R_\Delta:E\to E$ in the fixed coordinates, is
$$R_\Delta(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x=0,\\ p(x)\,\Delta\bigl(x/p(x)\bigr),&x\ne0.\end{cases}$$
For $x\ne0$, the normalized vector $x/p(x)$ belongs to $\Sigma_p$, so this expression is defined. Put
$$B_p=\{x:p(x)<1\},\qquad \overline B_q=\{y:q(y)\le1\}.$$
At a differentiability point $x$, let $DR_\Delta(x):E\to E$ be the Fréchet derivative and set
$$j_\Delta(x)=|\det DR_\Delta(x)|.$$
At other points set $j_\Delta(x)=0$. Thus $j_\Delta$ is the absolute Jacobian, not a norm of $R_\Delta(x)$ or a determinant of the nonlinear map itself. Then
$$\int_{B_p} j_\Delta(x)\,d\lambda(x)=\lambda(\overline B_q),$$
where the finite measure on the right is identified with its real value.
content.assumptions:
The dimension is the positive integer $n=m+1$. The maps defining $p$ and $q$ are continuous seminorms with the displayed positive comparison bounds. The sphere map $\Delta$ is a bijective isometry for the distances induced by $p$ and $q$.

The derivative and the measure in the integral use the fixed coordinate space $(E,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$, whereas the unit spheres use $p$ and $q$. No linearity or everywhere differentiability of $R_\Delta$ is assumed.
content.conclusion:
The left side is the integral of the nonnegative function $j_\Delta$ over the open $p$-unit ball. At a differentiability point, with coordinate vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ and component functions $R_{\Delta,i}(x)=(R_\Delta(x))_i$, the integrand is explicitly
$$j_\Delta(x)=\left|\det\bigl(\partial_jR_{\Delta,i}(x)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le n}\right|,$$
$$\partial_jR_{\Delta,i}(x)=(DR_\Delta(x)e_j)_i.$$
The right side is the volume of the closed $q$-unit ball in the same coordinates. The theorem uses the absolute Jacobian and does not assert that the radial extension is linear.
content.proof_summary: Prove global Lipschitz control and the exact open-ball image. Apply the nonnegative area formula after removing the null nondifferentiability set, justify the real integral, and use the zero-measure boundary of the target ball.

proof_steps.text:
**Control the map and identify its image.** Radius preservation and the inverse radial extension give
$$q(R_\Delta(x))=p(x),\qquad R_{\Delta^{-1}}(R_\Delta(x))=x\qquad(x\in E).$$
In particular, $R_\Delta$ is injective. The radial three-Lipschitz estimate and the comparison bounds give
$$\begin{aligned}
q(R_\Delta(x)-R_\Delta(x'))&\le3p(x-x'),\\
\|R_\Delta(x)-R_\Delta(x')\|_\infty&\le\frac{3b_p}{a_q}\|x-x'\|_\infty.
\end{aligned}$$
This is [the reference-coordinate Lipschitz bound](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Sphere/RadialJacobian.lean#L48-L62) for the same $p,q,\Delta$. Define the open target ball $B_q=\{y:q(y)<1\}$. The radius identity gives $R_\Delta(B_p)\subseteq B_q$. Conversely, for $y\in B_q$, take $x=R_{\Delta^{-1}}(y)$; then $p(x)=q(y)<1$ and $R_\Delta(x)=y$. Hence
$$R_\Delta(B_p)=B_q,$$
as stated by [the exact open-ball image theorem](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Sphere/RadialBall.lean#L137-L153).

**Remove null complements on the source and target.** Set
$$G=B_p\cap\{x:R_\Delta\text{ is differentiable at }x\},\qquad N=B_p\setminus G.$$
Then
$$\lambda(N)=0,\qquad \lambda(R_\Delta(N))=0.$$
The first is [Rademacher's theorem](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/360da6fa66c1273b76b6b2d8c5666fd5ac2e3b56/Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/Rademacher.lean#L387-L390) applied to the Lipschitz bound of Step 1. The second is [the equal-dimensional Lipschitz null-image theorem](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Calculus/BilipschitzOrientation/Basic.lean#L80-L97) for that same map and the null set $N$; it is recorded in [the radial image-exception lemma](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Sphere/RadialJacobian.lean#L137-L142). The set $G$ is measurable. Since $R_\Delta$ is injective and $R_\Delta(B_p)=B_q$,
$$B_q\setminus R_\Delta(G)=R_\Delta(N).$$
Thus the omitted target subset is null and $\lambda(R_\Delta(G))=\lambda(B_q)$.

**Apply the nonnegative area formula.** Write $\int^+$ for the nonnegative extended integral, valued in $[0,\infty]$. The formula is
$$\int_G^{+}j_\Delta(x)\,d\lambda(x)=\lambda(R_\Delta(G)).$$
Apply [the injective nonnegative area formula](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/360da6fa66c1273b76b6b2d8c5666fd5ac2e3b56/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/Jacobian.lean#L1094-L1103) with measurable domain $G$, map $R_\Delta$, derivative $DR_\Delta(x)$ at each $x\in G$, injectivity from Step 1, and reference Lebesgue measure $\lambda$. Step 2 then yields
$$\int_{B_p}^{+}j_\Delta\,d\lambda=\int_G^{+}j_\Delta\,d\lambda=\lambda(R_\Delta(G))=\lambda(B_q).$$
The first equality uses $\lambda(B_p\setminus G)=0$. These are extended nonnegative integrals; real integrability is established next.

**Verify integrability of the same integrand.** Put $\overline B_p=\{x:p(x)\le1\}$. This is compact by the comparison bounds. The integrability estimate is
$$\int_{\overline B_p}j_\Delta(x)\,d\lambda(x)=\int_{\overline B_p}|\det DR_\Delta(x)|\,d\lambda(x)<\infty.$$
For [compact-set integrability of Lipschitz derivative minors](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/MeasureTheory/Integral/MaximalMinor.lean#L102-L121), use $R_\Delta$, its reference-coordinate Lipschitz bound, the compact set $\overline B_p$, and all $n=m+1$ coordinates in increasing order. The resulting minor is $\det DR_\Delta$; taking the absolute value gives $j_\Delta$. This application is recorded by [integrability of the radial absolute determinant](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Sphere/RadialJacobian.lean#L144-L163). Since $B_p\subseteq\overline B_p$, we have $j_\Delta\in L^1(B_p,\lambda)$.

Because $j_\Delta\ge0$, its finite extended integral is the same number as its real integral. Taking real values in Step 3 therefore gives
$$\int_{B_p}j_\Delta(x)\,d\lambda(x)=\lambda(B_q),$$
with the finite measure on the right read as a real number.

**Replace the open target ball by the closed ball.** The boundary identities are
$$\partial B_q=\{y:q(y)=1\},\qquad \lambda(\partial B_q)=0,$$
$$\overline B_q=B_q\cup\partial B_q,\qquad \lambda(\overline B_q)=\lambda(B_q)<\infty.$$
The boundary description follows from the norm-ball description; its measure is zero by the convex-set boundary theorem. Both steps are used in [the open/closed target-volume lemma](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Sphere/RadialJacobian.lean#L223-L243). Finiteness follows from compactness of the closed $q$-unit ball. Substitution into Step 4 gives the stated equality
$$\int_{B_p}j_\Delta(x)\,d\lambda(x)=\lambda(\overline B_q).$$

content.lean_realization_notes: Changing from the norm $p$ or $q$ to the sup norm changes the normed-space structure, not the coordinate vector. The reference Lebesgue normalization remains fixed. At a point without a derivative, the source takes the zero linear map; since $n=m+1>0$, its determinant is zero, exactly matching the definition of $j_\Delta$ above.
